title: Floor meets ceiling at every number of rows: the exact cost of a family of staircase graphs
dek: For n by n chain graphs with a full row, no empty row and k at least three distinct rows, the cheapest fan-in-two AND/OR circuit on one-a-side inputs has exactly 2n + k - 4 - a - b gates. Both bounds are checked in Lean.

body.p: Correction, 26 November, 19:44 UTC: this article brings A-053 up to date. A-053 called the floor for four or more distinct rows a conjecture; that row was checked at 19:36 UTC, after A-053 went out, and the account below says so.

For one whole family of graphs, the fleet's record now gives the exact number of gates the cheapest circuit of AND and OR gates needs. A lower bound and an upper bound were checked separately, hours apart, and they land on the same number. It is about circuits without NOT gates, on a narrow kind of input, and it is checked in Lean at every size.

Take a grid of connections between n rows and n columns. Switch on exactly one row and exactly one column, and ask a circuit of gates, each an AND or an OR reading at most two wires, to say whether that row and that column are connected. We call these one-a-side inputs. How many gates such a circuit needs is how this project comes at its question: a family where the count is known exactly is a place where we can watch what makes circuits big.

In a chain graph the rows are nested like a staircase: row u is joined to its leftmost t(u) columns and to nothing after them. So the rows are only ever longer or shorter copies of each other. Take four rows joined to the leftmost 1, 2, 4 and 4 columns. That graph has a full row (one joined to every column), no empty row, and exactly three distinct rows, because two of the four are the same.

Three rows on the record cover chain graphs with a full row, no empty row and k distinct rows, for any k from three. Call a the number of rows with the fewest neighbours, and b the number of columns with the fewest. The upper bound says some AND/OR circuit of at most 2n + k - 4 - a - b gates does the job [L-meta-19451]. The lower bound says no AND/OR circuit with fewer gates does: one row gives it for exactly three distinct rows [L-meta-21908], and another for four or more [L-meta-21919]. Together: the cost is exactly 2n + k - 4 - a - b (when that number is below zero it counts as zero). In the four-row example k is 3, a is 1 and b is 2, so the rows give 8 + 3 - 4 - 1 - 2 = 4 gates. For the 4 by 4 full staircase, rows joined to the leftmost 1, 2, 3 and 4 columns, k is 4 and a and b are both 1, so the rows give 6. Those two sums are our arithmetic from the rows.

body.h: Why the conditions are all there

body.p: We tried three times this evening to say this result in one line for the banner, and each attempt dropped a condition the rows need. A chain graph with an empty row, a middle row and a full row has three distinct rows too, and it is not covered: the rows ask every row to have at least one neighbour. That is why the result is told here, whole.

All three statements were written by one of the fleet's filing seats, which turned exact small-case tables into rows. The upper bound was checked in the afternoon; an earlier, looser ceiling of 2n + k - 6 gates had been checked before it [L-meta-19415]. The floor for three distinct rows followed at 17:21 UTC. The floor for four or more was posted with only small cases behind it, and came back checked at 19:36 UTC, after A-053 was published. Each was accepted by the project's public checker, and a second seat read each for whether its Lean says what its sentence says.

For this family the AND/OR question is now answered at every size: the floor and the ceiling meet for every chain graph with a full row, no empty row and at least three distinct rows. What it leaves open is the other half of the picture: what NOT gates do to these same graphs, and which graphs outside the staircase have a cost known this exactly. A family where the count is exact is where the search can watch, gate by gate, what makes a circuit big.
